cards.question: Tp ÷ (Tp + Tsched)
cards.answer: CPU utilization: fraction of CPU time spent on useful work. Tp = timeslice (time a process runs on the CPU); Tsched = time the scheduler takes to run.
cards.memory: P2L1. Lecture form over two intervals: (2 × Tp) ÷ (2 × Tp + 2 × Tsched). Tp = Tsched → 50%. Tp = 10 × Tsched → 10/11 ≈ 91%.
distractors: Scheduler overhead: fraction of CPU time spent scheduling. Tp = timeslice; Tsched = time the scheduler takes to run.
CPU utilization. Tp = time the scheduler takes to run; Tsched = timeslice (time a process runs on the CPU).
Throughput. Tp = number of processes completed; Tsched = length of the scheduling period.

cards.question: 2^(number of address bits) bytes
cards.answer: Maximum size of a process's virtual address space (V0 to Vmax). Number of address bits = width of a virtual address.
cards.memory: P2L1: 32-bit virtual addresses → 2^32 bytes = 4 GB. Every process gets the full range; the OS maps each process's range to different physical memory. (The lecture gives the 32-bit example; 2^bits is the general rule behind it.)
distractors: Physical memory a process is actually using. Number of address bits = pages the process has touched.
Number of page table entries in a process. Number of address bits = size of one page.
Physical memory shared by all processes. Number of address bits = number of running processes.

cards.question: shared-memory setup cost ÷ number of messages
cards.answer: Amortized setup cost per message for shared-memory IPC; shared memory only pays off when enough messages make this small. Setup cost = cost of mapping the memory into both processes; number of messages = messages exchanged over the region.
cards.memory: P2L1 quiz: "it depends." Each exchange is cheap (no copying into/out of the kernel), but the mapping itself is expensive. (The lecture says this in words; the ratio is written out here.)
distractors: Cost of copying each message through the kernel. Setup cost = system call cost; number of messages = messages in the kernel buffer.
Number of messages that fit in the shared region. Setup cost = region size; number of messages = message size.
Context-switch cost per message. Setup cost = context-switch time; number of messages = messages per timeslice.

cards.question: t_idle > 2 × t_ctx_switch
cards.answer: Condition for when context switching to another thread (to hide idle time) is worthwhile. t_idle = time a thread would sit idle (e.g. waiting on disk I/O); t_ctx_switch = time for one context switch.
cards.memory: P2L2 (repeated in P2L5). ×2 = one switch away + one switch back. Thread switches are cheaper than process switches (no new virtual-to-physical mappings), so threads can hide more idle time.
distractors: Condition for when context switching is worthwhile. t_idle = time for one context switch; t_ctx_switch = time a thread waits on I/O.
Adaptive mutex rule for when to spin. t_idle = remaining critical-section time; t_ctx_switch = time to queue a thread.
Condition for a hot cache. t_idle = time since the process last ran; t_ctx_switch = cache refill time.

cards.question: process's CPU share ÷ number of user-level threads in that process
cards.answer: CPU share each user-level thread gets under process scope (the OS divides the CPU among processes, not threads). Process's CPU share = portion the OS gives the whole process; number of user-level threads = threads managed by that process's library.
cards.memory: P2L2: web server has 2× the threads of the database; the OS splits 50/50 → each web-server thread gets half the CPU cycles of a database thread.
distractors: CPU share each user-level thread gets under system scope. Process's CPU share = total CPU; number of user-level threads = threads across all processes.
Number of kernel-level threads a process needs. Process's CPU share = number of CPUs; number of user-level threads = threads that are blocked.
Throughput of the boss-worker model. Process's CPU share = boss time per order; number of user-level threads = workers.

cards.question: total CPU ÷ total user-level threads (across all processes)
cards.answer: CPU share each user-level thread gets under system scope (every thread is visible to the kernel and gets an equal share). Total CPU = all CPU time on the platform; total user-level threads = threads across every process.
cards.memory: P2L2. A process with more threads ends up with a larger total share of the CPU. (Equal share per thread assumes that is the kernel's policy.)
distractors: CPU share each user-level thread gets under process scope. Total CPU = the process's CPU share; total user-level threads = threads in that one process.
CPU utilization. Total CPU = timeslice; total user-level threads = number of scheduler runs.
Minimum threads needed to boot Linux. Total CPU = number of CPUs; total user-level threads = init threads.

cards.question: throughput ∝ 1 ÷ (boss time per order)
cards.answer: Boss-worker throughput is inversely proportional to how long the boss spends on each order. Boss time per order = time the boss thread spends accepting and handing off one order.
cards.memory: P2L2. Keep the boss efficient: a shared queue beats having the boss track which worker is free, because it cuts boss time per order.
distractors: Pipeline throughput is limited by the fastest stage. Boss time per order = time of the shortest stage.
Boss-worker throughput grows with how long the boss spends on each order. Boss time per order = time a worker takes per order.
Boss-worker average completion time. Boss time per order = time a worker takes per order.

cards.question: ⌈orders ÷ workers⌉ × time_per_order
cards.answer: Total execution time of the boss-worker model. orders = number of orders; workers = threads − 1 (one thread is the boss); time_per_order = time one worker takes to finish one order.
cards.memory: P2L2 quiz: 6 threads → 5 workers, 120 ms per toy. 10 orders: 2 × 120 = 240 ms. 11 orders: 3 × 120 = 360 ms.
distractors: Total execution time of the pipeline model. orders = number of orders; workers = number of stages; time_per_order = time per stage.
Average completion time in the boss-worker model. orders = number of orders; workers = threads; time_per_order = time per order.
Total execution time of the boss-worker model. orders = number of orders; workers = all threads including the boss; time_per_order = time the boss spends per order.

cards.question: (stages × stage_time) + (orders − 1) × stage_time
cards.answer: Total execution time of the pipeline model. stages = number of pipeline stages; stage_time = time per stage; orders = number of orders. First term = first order through every stage; each later order finishes one stage_time behind.
cards.memory: P2L2 quiz: 6 stages × 20 ms = 120 ms for the first order. 10 orders: 120 + 9 × 20 = 300 ms. 11 orders: 120 + 10 × 20 = 320 ms. Only works when every stage takes the same time; for unequal stages use (Σ stage_timeᵢ) + (N − 1) × balanced stage time.
distractors: Total execution time of the boss-worker model. stages = workers; stage_time = time per order; orders = number of orders.
Average completion time in the pipeline model. stages = number of stages; stage_time = time per stage; orders = number of orders.
Time for one order to pass through the pipeline. stages = number of stages; stage_time = time per stage; orders = orders waiting in the queue.

cards.question: stage_timeᵢ ÷ shortest stage_time
cards.answer: Number of threads to assign to pipeline stage i so every stage keeps pace (a balanced pipeline). stage_timeᵢ = time stage i takes with one thread; shortest stage_time = time of the fastest stage.
cards.memory: P2L2: wood-cutting takes 3× longer than the other stages → 3 threads. Midterm-style: stages of 10, 30, 20 ms → 1, 3, 2 threads. (The lecture gives the example; the ratio is written out here.)
distractors: Number of threads to assign to stage i. stage_timeᵢ = time of the fastest stage; shortest stage_time = time stage i takes.
Pipeline speedup over a single thread. stage_timeᵢ = total single-thread time; shortest stage_time = time per stage.
Fraction of time stage i sits idle. stage_timeᵢ = idle time of stage i; shortest stage_time = busy time.

cards.question: (Σ stage_timeᵢ) + (N − 1) × max(stage_timeᵢ ÷ threadsᵢ)
cards.answer: Total execution time of a pipeline with unequal stages. stage_timeᵢ = time stage i takes with one thread; threadsᵢ = threads assigned to stage i; N = number of requests. First term = first request through every stage; after that one request finishes every max(stage_timeᵢ ÷ threadsᵢ), the slowest effective stage.
cards.memory: Midterm-style: stages of 10, 30, 20 ms with 1, 3, 2 threads → every stage effectively 10 ms. 100 requests: 60 + 99 × 10 = 1,050 ms = 1.05 s. With 1 thread per stage the bottleneck is 30 ms: 60 + 99 × 30 = 3,030 ms.
distractors: Total execution time of the boss-worker model. stage_timeᵢ = time per worker; threadsᵢ = workers; N = number of requests.
Average completion time per request in a pipeline. stage_timeᵢ = time of stage i; threadsᵢ = threads in stage i; N = number of requests.
Total pipeline execution time. stage_timeᵢ = time of stage i; threadsᵢ = threads in stage i; N = number of stages.

cards.question: stage_timeᵢ ÷ threadsᵢ
cards.answer: Effective time per request for pipeline stage i once it has several threads; the largest of these sets the pipeline pace. stage_timeᵢ = time stage i takes with one thread; threadsᵢ = threads assigned to stage i.
cards.memory: 30 ms stage with 3 threads → one request leaves every 10 ms. Pipeline throughput is set by the weakest link (longest effective stage).
distractors: Number of threads to assign to stage i. stage_timeᵢ = time of stage i; threadsᵢ = time of the fastest stage.
Total execution time of stage i. stage_timeᵢ = time of stage i; threadsᵢ = number of requests.
CPU share per thread in stage i. stage_timeᵢ = CPU time of stage i; threadsᵢ = threads in the process.

cards.question: N requests ÷ total execution time
cards.answer: Average throughput of a server run (requests per second). N requests = number of requests processed; total execution time = time to finish all N (convert ms → s).
cards.memory: Midterm-style pipeline: 100 requests ÷ 1.05 s ≈ 95.2 req/s. As N grows it approaches 1 ÷ (bottleneck stage time) = 1 ÷ 0.010 s = 100 req/s.
distractors: Average time per request. N requests = total execution time; total execution time = number of requests.
Connection rate. N requests = connections serviced; total execution time = file size.
Bandwidth. N requests = bytes sent; total execution time = transfer time.

cards.question: (in + 1) mod N = out
cards.answer: Circular buffer is full (the next slot to write is the next slot to read). in = index of the next slot to write; out = index of the next item to read; N = buffer size (BUFFERSIZE).
cards.memory: This convention always leaves one slot empty, so the buffer holds at most N − 1 items. That slot is how "full" is told apart from "empty" (in = out). The P2L3 lecture tracks a count, num, instead: full when num = N.
distractors: Circular buffer is empty. in = index of the next slot to write; out = index of the next item to read; N = buffer size.
Index of the next slot after in. in = current write index; out = read index; N = buffer size.
Number of items in the buffer. in = write index; out = read index; N = buffer size.

cards.question: in = out
cards.answer: Circular buffer is empty (nothing between the read and write positions). in = index of the next slot to write; out = index of the next item to read.
cards.memory: Pairs with full: (in + 1) mod N = out. The P2L3 lecture uses num = 0 for empty instead.
distractors: Circular buffer is full. in = write index; out = read index.
Producer and consumer are deadlocked. in = producers waiting; out = consumers waiting.
Buffer index wrapped around to 0. in = write index; out = buffer size.

cards.question: (i + 1) mod N
cards.answer: Next index in a circular buffer, wrapping back to 0 after the last slot. i = current index (in or out); N = buffer size.
cards.memory: P2L3: add and rem both advance this way ("modular computation to deal with wrap-arounds"). N = 3 in the lecture: 0 → 1 → 2 → 0.
distractors: Number of items in the buffer. i = write index; N = buffer size.
Circular buffer is full. i = write index; N = read index.
Number of threads for a pipeline stage. i = stage time; N = shortest stage time.

cards.question: (in − out + N) mod N
cards.answer: Number of items currently in a circular buffer. in = index of the next slot to write; out = index of the next item to read; N = buffer size.
cards.memory: Plays the role of the lecture's num counter. + N keeps the result non-negative when in has wrapped around past out.
distractors: Number of free slots in the buffer. in = write index; out = read index; N = buffer size.
Next index in the buffer. in = current index; out = step size; N = buffer size.
Circular buffer is full. in = write index; out = read index; N = buffer size.

cards.question: time for the mutex owner to release < time to context switch and queue the waiting thread
cards.answer: Adaptive mutex rule: spin instead of block (only when the owner is running on another CPU). Time for the owner to release = remaining critical-section time; time to context switch and queue = cost of blocking the waiting thread.
cards.memory: P2L4: short critical sections → spin; long → block. Only makes sense on multi-CPU systems. (The lecture says this in words; the inequality is written out here.)
distractors: Condition for when context switching to hide idle time is worthwhile. Time for the owner to release = I/O wait time; time to context switch = one switch.
Adaptive mutex rule: block instead of spin. Time for the owner to release = remaining critical-section time; time to context switch and queue = cost of blocking.
Condition for a deadlock. Time for the owner to release = lock hold time; time to context switch and queue = wait time.

cards.question: (12 × mutex_ops) − (40 × interrupts)
cards.answer: Net instructions saved by Solaris handling interrupts as threads. mutex_ops = number of mutex lock/unlock operations; interrupts = number of interrupts; 12 = instructions saved per mutex op (no interrupt-mask change); 40 = instructions added per interrupt (checks + possibly creating a thread).
cards.memory: P2L4. Mutex ops vastly outnumber interrupts → net win. Lesson: optimize for the common case.
distractors: Net instructions saved by Solaris handling interrupts as threads. mutex_ops = number of interrupts; interrupts = number of mutex operations; 12 = cost per interrupt; 40 = savings per mutex op.
Instructions spent on context switches between threads. mutex_ops = switches; interrupts = timer ticks; 12 = cost per switch; 40 = cost per tick.
Net cost of disabling interrupts in critical sections. mutex_ops = critical sections; interrupts = masked interrupts; 12 = mask cost; 40 = handler cost.

cards.question: thread index × size of thread data structure
cards.answer: Offset for finding a user-level thread's data structure in Solaris's contiguous layout. Thread index = the thread ID (an index into a table); size of thread data structure = fixed size known at compile time.
cards.memory: P2L4 (Stein & Shah). Contiguous layout → locality, and the scheduler finds a thread with one multiply. Red zones between structures catch stack overflows.
distractors: Total stack space for all threads. Thread index = number of threads; size of thread data structure = stack size.
Size of the red zone between two threads. Thread index = thread priority; size of thread data structure = page size.
Number of lightweight processes the kernel creates. Thread index = concurrency level; size of thread data structure = LWP size.

cards.question: signal raised n times → handler runs n times
cards.answer: Real-time signals (e.g. Linux): queuing behavior. n = number of times the signal is raised.
distractors: One-shot signals: overriding behavior. n = number of times the signal is raised.
Interrupts: every instance is handled by the top half. n = number of interrupts.
Masked signals: they are delivered once the mask is cleared. n = number of pending signals.

cards.question: signal raised n times → handler runs at least once (maybe only once)
cards.answer: One-shot signals: overriding behavior, and the custom handler must be re-installed after each use. n = number of times the signal is raised.
distractors: Real-time signals: queuing behavior. n = number of times the signal is raised.
Interrupts handled as threads. n = number of interrupts.
Signals sent to a multithreaded process: one per thread. n = number of threads.

cards.question: (sum of each order's completion time) ÷ number of orders
cards.answer: Average time to complete an order (the metric customers care about). Completion time = time from start until that order finishes; number of orders = total orders in the workload.
cards.memory: P2L5, 11 toy orders. Boss-worker: (5 × 120 + 5 × 240 + 360) ÷ 11 ≈ 196 ms. Pipeline: (120 + 140 + … + 320) ÷ 11 = 220 ms. Boss-worker wins on average time, pipeline wins on total time.
distractors: Total execution time. Completion time = time per stage; number of orders = number of stages.
Throughput. Completion time = time period; number of orders = orders completed.
Metric averaged over repeated experiment runs. Completion time = metric per run; number of orders = number of runs.

cards.question: tasks completed ÷ time period
cards.answer: Throughput. Tasks completed = number of tasks/processes/jobs finished; time period = length of the measurement window.
cards.memory: P2L5. Measures a platform's utility (one server or a whole data center). What a toy-shop manager or data center operator cares about.
distractors: Connection rate. Tasks completed = client connections serviced; time period = measurement window.
Response time. Tasks completed = requests answered; time period = time per request.
CPU utilization. Tasks completed = useful CPU time; time period = total CPU time.

cards.question: throughput ÷ resources used
cards.answer: Platform efficiency: how well resources are used to deliver throughput. Throughput = tasks completed per time period; resources used = servers/cost consumed to deliver it.
cards.memory: P2L5. Data center operator: throughput brings income, but machines cost money, so the ratio matters. (The lecture describes this in words; the ratio is written out here.)
distractors: Performance per dollar. Throughput = performance; resources used = hardware price.
CPU utilization. Throughput = useful CPU time; resources used = total CPU time.
Percentage of SLA violations. Throughput = violating requests; resources used = total requests.

cards.question: performance ÷ cost
cards.answer: Performance per dollar: whether the extra cost of new hardware is worth the performance gain. Performance = the chosen performance metric; cost = price in dollars.
distractors: Performance per watt. Performance = chosen metric; cost = power delivered in watts.
Platform efficiency. Performance = throughput; cost = resources used.
Performance per joule. Performance = chosen metric; cost = energy consumed.

cards.question: performance ÷ power
cards.answer: Performance per watt. Performance = the chosen performance metric; power = watts delivered to the platform.
distractors: Performance per joule. Performance = chosen metric; power = energy consumed during execution.
Performance per dollar. Performance = chosen metric; power = price of the hardware.
Bandwidth. Performance = bytes transferred; power = transfer time.

cards.question: performance ÷ energy
cards.answer: Performance per joule. Performance = the chosen performance metric; energy = joules consumed during execution.
distractors: Performance per watt. Performance = chosen metric; energy = power delivered to the platform.
Performance per dollar. Performance = chosen metric; energy = price of the hardware.
Platform efficiency. Performance = throughput; energy = resources used.

cards.question: (requests violating the SLA ÷ total requests) × 100
cards.answer: Percentage of SLA (Service Level Agreement) violations. Requests violating the SLA = requests that missed the agreed target; total requests = all requests served.
cards.memory: P2L5. Example SLAs: "response within 3 seconds", or "accurate quotes for 95% of flights."
distractors: 95th-percentile response time. Requests violating the SLA = slowest 5% of requests; total requests = all requests.
Connection rate. Requests violating the SLA = connections serviced; total requests = time period.
CPU utilization. Requests violating the SLA = busy time; total requests = total time.

cards.question: (n × file_size) ÷ time to process the n requests
cards.answer: Web server bandwidth in bytes/second (Flash paper). n = number of requests; file_size = bytes in the requested file.
cards.memory: P2L5 Flash best-case experiment: every request is for the same file; file size varied 0–200 KB. Bigger files amortize connection cost → higher bandwidth.
distractors: Connection rate. n = connections serviced; file_size = connection overhead.
Throughput in requests per second. n = number of requests; file_size = requests per connection.
Average response time. n = number of requests; file_size = bytes per response.

cards.question: client connections serviced ÷ time period
cards.answer: Connection rate (Flash paper). Client connections serviced = number of client connections handled; time period = measurement window.
cards.memory: P2L5. Evaluated against file size: larger files mean more work per connection, which can lower the connection rate.
distractors: Bandwidth. Client connections serviced = bytes sent; time period = transfer time.
Percentage of SLA violations. Client connections serviced = violating requests; time period = total requests.
Platform efficiency. Client connections serviced = throughput; time period = resources used.

cards.question: (metric₁ + metric₂ + … + metricₙ) ÷ n
cards.answer: The value to report for a metric: its average over n repeated runs of an experiment. metricₖ = value measured in run k; n = number of runs.
cards.memory: P2L5, advice on running experiments: run each test case n times, then compute the averages.
distractors: Average order completion time. metricₖ = completion time of order k; n = number of orders.
Throughput. metricₖ = tasks finished in second k; n = seconds measured.
Priority-weighted average execution time. metricₖ = time of task k; n = sum of the priorities.

cards.question: Σ (priorityₖ × timeₖ) ÷ Σ priorityₖ
cards.answer: Aggregate performance metric: the priority-weighted average of execution (or wait) time across all tasks. priorityₖ = priority (weight) of task k; timeₖ = execution or wait time of task k.
cards.memory: P2L5. The lecture mentions averaging execution or wait time over all tasks, "or maybe even a weighted average based on the priorities." (The formula is written out here.)
distractors: Metric averaged over repeated runs. priorityₖ = run number; timeₖ = metric measured in run k.
Average order completion time. priorityₖ = order number; timeₖ = completion time of order k.
Percentage of SLA violations. priorityₖ = SLA target; timeₖ = response time of request k.

cards.question: time the job starts executing − time the job was submitted
cards.answer: Wait time: how long a user waits before their job actually starts running.
cards.memory: P2L5. Matters for interactive jobs, and for long jobs (start early → spot problems early). (The lecture defines it in words; the subtraction is written out here.)
distractors: Response time: how long until the job's result comes back.
Execution time: how long the job runs on the CPU.
Timeslice: how long the job may run before it is preempted.
